responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

One Life between Two People: Some Themes from the Analysis of a Nine-to-Fifteen-Year-Old Anorexic Girl

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

120, Belsize Lane
London N.W.3.

Maria Rhode  

Laura, the anorexic girl I wish to discuss in this paper, came to analysis just before her ninth birthday. After three and a half years, we cut down to twice weekly treatment while I was expecting a baby, then resumed once weekly after a break of nearly a year. When Laura stopped treatment some months ago, on her fifteenth birthday, she had been coming to see me for just over six years.

In the two years before I qualified, I was supervised by Mrs. Martha Harris, whom I wish to thank for her help. I wish also to express my thanks to Dr. Donald Meltzer for some discussions since then, and to Dr. H.S. Klein.

It is difficult to describe Laura's material without giving a very wrong idea of the atmosphere in her sessions. In the early years particularly, they were filled with incessant activity and yet they seemed frozen: a whole week's material fitted easily into a single supervision. At the same time, I felt that she would take a transfer very badly, as though my continuous experience of her were somehow vitally important. The content of her material fitted with this feeling, in the sense that themes concerning life and death were prominent. Her manner, however, was that of a cheerful, chatty, verbally precocious nine-year-old: I felt I had met with the perfect embodiment of the concept of false self. She was at that time very undersized for her age, and terribly thin. Her brown hair was scraped back into a pony-tail: one could see through her skin to the veins on her forehead. Somehow her features looked blurred: she reminded me of pictures of the head of a foetus.

Throughout Laura's treatment, there was conveyed to me a sense of impending birth, of a step towards something new that was just about to take place. Looking back, in fact, I see that most themes that later proved important had already been clearly stated in the first months—and in terms implying as “deep” a level as we ever reached subsequently. Nothing new was “born” on the level of content. What did change—though with utter and painful slowness—was the degree to which the content could be brought within the transference relationship.

[[RunningHead]]

Brief Psychotherapy with a Three-Year-Old Girl11

“You Don't Want to Touch That Hole, Do You?”

Ellen Jaffe

Ellen Jaffe

120, Belsize Lane
London N.W.3.

Ellen Jaffe  

In child guidance clinics, particularly in areas unfamiliar with child psychotherapy, we are often able to offer only limited or short-term help to a child who might require intensive psychotherapy. This is especially likely to happen when the child's immediate environment is unsettled: parents may be unable to support the treatment; they may move away; the child may be taken into care or sent to boarding school; or similar outside events may terminate therapy prematurely. If, at the referral, we know that time available is limited, we must assess carefully whether to undertake therapy at all. This is true even though the child may unquestionably be in deep psychic pain. We must ask ourselves if the breaking of yet another relationship will do more harm than good, or if, on the contrary, the opportunity to explore feelings and fantasies, including those of sadness, anger, loss and helplessness, will help the child to develop and to cope with new changes.

In this paper, I will discuss a three-year-old girl, Rachel, whom I saw twice weekly for psychotherapy during a period of ten weeks, 19 sessions in all, just before she and her mother moved to another city. Her mother met weekly with a clinic social worker.

Background

I first saw Rachel in September. Her mother (Mrs. G.) had been attending the clinic since March of that year, when she had sought help on behalf of her daughter, who at the time (age 2 years, 7 months) was existing almost entirely on warm milk from a bottle, usually fed by mother (2-4 bottles a day). She was not using the pot or toilet. Rachel was an only child, and Mrs. G., age 30, was separated from her husband, who was not Rachel's father. After several years of a tenuous marriage, she had become pregnant by a married Spanish man, who had no intention of leaving his own family. (Mrs. G. and her husband are English.) Mrs. G. saw her affair primarily as a way of finding out if she could become pregnant and of having a child.

She left her husband during pregnancy but returned before Rachel's birth. As far as I know, Rachel has never seen her natural father. Mr. G. never attended the clinic.

Correspondence

Mental Health Care in South Africa

A. Jablensky

A. Jablensky

1211 Geneva 27, Switzerland

A. Jablensky  

In 1978 this journal (Vol. 4, No. 4) published an “Open Letter” in which Dr. James MacKeith drew attention to the ethical problems arising from the publication of the World Health Organization's Preliminary Review, “Apartheid and Mental Health Care”. Dr. MacKeith suggested that his comments be sent to the South African Minister of Health for forwarding to psychiatrists with “direct clinical responsibility for the services concerned”. In writing to the South African Minister of Health, the editor drew attention to Dr. MacKeith's suggestion, and added that this journal would be happy to publish informed and free comment.

The Acting Minister of Health's reply is given below; in it he refers to the correspondence in “The Lancet” on this topic. In order that readers may judge this issue for themselves we also give below the two major letters from the correspondence in “The Lancet”: that of Professor Gillis, which attacks the views of the W.H.O. preliminary review, and that of jablensky which supports those views.

12th July 1978

Dear Madam,

I write to reply to your letter of 19th May 1978 together with enclosure, the contents of which have been noted.

May I express appreciation of Dr. MacKeith's efforts in endeavouring to obtain objectivity on an emotionally-ridden subject.

I should however, like to draw your attention to an editorial on the World Health Organisation Report “Apartheid and Mental Health Care”, which appeared in “The Lancet” of 3rd September 1977, and which was fully replied to by Professor L.S. Gillis in his capacity as Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Society of Psychiatrists of South Africa. I wish to assure you that this and subsequent lengthy correspondence which appeared in the columns of “The Lancet”, was free, unsolicited comment and was at no time referred to me for approval in terms of any existing legislation.

Journals such as yours are freely available to the interested disciplines in this country and members are at liberty to react to their contents in a manner they deem fit.

responseSet.title: A Child's Personal Questions—What Do They Mean?
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Child's Personal Questions—What Do They Mean?

Carole Litt

Carole Litt

Hanna Pavilion
2040 Abington Road
Cleveland
Ohio 44106.

Carole Litt  

The issues of what to do when a child asks personal questions about a therapist and his life is one which has received little attention in the literature. The subject is raised only briefly in a few manuals for beginning psychotherapists. In the majority of cases the implication is that personal questions arise as the result of resistance to therapy and should be handled in much the same way one would interpret such questions from an adult. Advice on how to deal with such questions runs the gamut from Ginott's (1964) succinct “no autobiography” (p. 129) to Ross' (1964) more considered admonition that cutting off a child's questioning by interpreting the unconscious reasons for it may inhibit the child's natural press to explore his world and find his place in it. It is, after all, a therapist's job to help the child with both his unconscious conflicts and his ego development. Ross does suggest, however, that the therapist should first give the child a chance to explore his fantasies and wishes regarding the question before providing factual information. The latter should be given only if the child continues to repeat the question. He further cautions the therapist to check for the child's own thoughts and information before answering questions regarding sex or religious beliefs. This is necessary so as to avoid bringing the therapist's own views into confusng conflict with those taught by the parents.

Swanson (1970) points out that there are exceptions to the general rule that questions of children, especially those with neurotic disturbances, should be met with an inquiry as to why the child is asking. She feels that both schizoid and brain-injured children need the help of straight-forward factual answers in order to help confirm accurate perceptions of reality. They benefit from always hearing the same truthful answer, no matter how many times they ask.

In considering the significance of a child's questions, one must recall Freud's (1907) classic observation that a child's first experience with intellectual problem solving often begins with his effort to solve the mystery of his own origins. A child's failure to resolve this mystery due to the withholding of information by adults may have a crippling effect on his future intellectual as well as emotional development. Freud advises us that there is no virtue in withholding desired sexual information from children, for secrecy only serves to further inflame curiosity and lead the child to distorted and “corrupting” beliefs. He further warns that giving evasive answers may “wound the child's frank and genuine spirit of investigation, and generally deal the first blow at his confidence inhis parents; from this time onwards he commonly begins to mistrust grown-up people and keeps to himself what interests him most”. (p. 40).

Child AbuseRuth S. Kempe and C. Henry Kempe (London, Fontana/Open Books, £ 1.25)

Dorothy Luciani

Dorothy Luciani

Dorothy Luciani  

Child Abuse is one in a series of books subtitled, “The Developing Child”, edited by Jerome Bruner, Michael Cole, and Barbara Lloyd. The series is designed to make information on recent research in child development available to all people who deal with children. Judging from Child Abuse and another book which I have read in the series (Distress and Comfort by Judy Dunn) the books appear to be of high quality, informative, helpful and thought-provoking.

The Kempes' small, highly readable book speaks with authority on the subject of child abuse. It is based on twenty years of study at the National Center for the Prevention and Treatment of Child Abuse at the University of Colorado School of Medicine. Over the years 3,000 families have been treated at the Center. The Kempes claim that 4 out of 5 families were helped; surely a cause for optimism in a field where despair often prevails. Their book describes, clearly and comprehensively, the authors' understanding of the parents and children they have seen and the treatment approaches they have used. Each page is filled with information and practical suggestions. The last chapter of the book contains guidelines for the establishment of a community-wide approach to the problem of child abuse among which is the idea that the social worker is the natural leader of a child abuse team and should be assisted by a pediatrician, health visitor, lawyer, psychologist and psychiatrist, all equal in status. Compassion for the child, his parents, and the people who work with them informs the book from beginning to end.

When writing about the abusive parent the authors point out that in order to become an adequate parent one must have been cherished and nurtured in early life, in the time before memory and speech. As we know, many parents who abuse their children were abused themselves, either emotionally or physically. Taking a slightly different angle on this well known fact, the Kempes give us an insight into what drives the abusive parent: “… it seems to us that the tenacity with which parents cling to their parenting behaviour owes its strength to the threats to survival they themselves experienced in the time before memory”. The lack of nurturance which these parents experience cannot be ignored. The authors find that if the parents' deep seated needs are not taken into consideration, if one focuses only on parental responsibilities, the parents are likely to become more abusive. They go on to formulate four factors which must combine in the parents' lives before abuse occurs: (1) The parents must have a background of emotional or physical deprivation and perhaps abuse as well; (2) they must see their child as unlovable and disappointing; (3) there must be a crisis; and (4) there must be no effective line of communication to help. The fourth factor is underlined as the determining factor in child abuse.

[[RunningHead]]

Transference in the Residential Treatment of Children11

Christopher Radlett

Christopher Radlett

23, Canons Close
Radlett
Herts
U.K

Christopher Radlett  

In this paper I want to bring together certain familiar concepts of traditional psychoanalytic theory—concepts such as the repetition compulsion, the function of play in transforming passive experiences into active expression, and the role of transference in the therapeutic process—with some working principles which have informed the efforts of one of the best known British schools for junior school-age maladjusted children, the Mulberry Bush School. The attempt to do so reflects my personal efforts to synthesize my experiences and background as a child psychotherapist with the perspectives and challenges opened up when I took on the post of Therapeutic Adviser to this school in succession to its founder, Mrs. Dockar Drysdale. It should be as a first foray rather than a systematic expedition into territory which, with the exception of a few classics (e.g. Aichorn, 1935; Bettelheim, 1950; Redl, 1951) has been little explored by psychodynamic theorists.

The children we are trying to help at The Mulberry Bush School are those suffering from the lack of what Winnicott has called ‘primary maternal preoccupation’ (Winnicott 1958); that is, from a breakdown of the emotional sustenance from the mothering person on which the psychic health of the infant depends. In other words, we are dealing with children whose original trauma or series of traumas occurred at a time when they were incapable of registering the events which affected them as memories. The fact that these crucial events took place before they could be registered as memories does not mean that they do not have active symbolic expression in the child's behaviour. On the contrary, the fact that the events could not be memorized—we might more properly say conceptualized—is a principal reason why they are likely to be expressed in disguised symbolic form through the child's behaviour. We might even go so far as to say that such children have not reached the stage of limited integration exhibited by Freud's two year old grandchild in his famous example of the play with the string and the bobbin (Freud, 1920). They are incapable, that is to say, of playing out conflicts instead of acting them out.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Question of Autism

P. Radford

P. Radford

The Hampstead Clinic
12, Maresfield Gdns.
London N.W.3.

P. Radford  

A boy of three was presented to the Clinic for a diagnostic assessment because he was showing signs of autism. I, as diagnostician, was of the opinion that while David was not yet autistic, there were possibilities that he might end as if he were. I will try to indicate the vulnerable aspects of his personality as described by his parents and by colleagues who referred him for assessment. I shall give my metapsychological understanding of the case based on the diagnostic material, making use of the format of Anna Freud's Profile. I shall then attempt to show from his ongoing analytic treatment how far my opinion was validated and to what, if any, extent David was in danger of being seen as a child with secondary autism. I shall attempt to pin-point those areas of his personality which seem at risk.

Kanner first drew attention to the condition he called autism. He defined it as an inate inability to perform the usual biologically provided, affective contact with people. He noted that most of the children whom he diagnosed had intellectual parents who failed to understand what babies need. (Kanner 1943). Winnicott considered that childhood psychosis, in which he included autism, was an environmental deficiency disease (Winnicott 1976). Francis Tustin implied that psychotic states are developmental phenomena arising through interference with normal processes (Tustin 1966). Margaret Mahler (1975) described infantile autism (and symbiotic psychosis) as an extreme disturbance of identity, of awareness of a sense of being, a feeling that includes a cathexis of the body with libidinal energy—not ‘who I am’, but ‘that I am’. She considered that, “the psychotic child never attains a feeling of wholeness, of individual entity, let alone a sense of human identity. In autism and symbiotic infantile psychosis, something has gone basically astray at the very root, that is in the earliest interactions within the mother/infant unit”. In primary autism a de-animated frozen wall exists between the subject and the human object. Mahler (1975) and Francis Tustin (1969) described these children as fixated to bodily experiences, able to experience feeling life only through good or bad body sensations, as failure in their object relationships prevented their using normal mothering to orientate themselves in reality.

[[RunningHead]]

An Analytic Intervention in the Life of a Girl Growing up in a Chaotic Environment

“Why are My Glasses So Hot?”

Helga Deaton

Helga Deaton

22, Lower Redland Road
Bristol BS6 6SU.

Helga Deaton  

Introduction

There is no doubt that Peggy, with whom I began treatment when she was just four- and-a-half, is one of those children who have been born into and have had to grow up in an almost intolerable environment. To the extent to which I have experienced and have been exposed to the reality of this environment I have often felt upset and helpless, at times angry, sometimes even psychologically battered. On such occasions of upset I had to remind myself that I was able to deal with these experiences as a grownup and at a remove, and that they were not part of my own daily life as they were of Peggy's. How then, I often wondered, was Peggy able to handle and to deal with these experiences and this reality? It was also on such occasions that my protective feelings towards Peggy became very strong. Nothing in her environment is either ‘average’ or ‘expectable’. The problems of this outer world, extreme, uncertain and unreliable, are greater than the problems of her inner world, which without doubt also exist.

During the diagnostic discussion in which Peggy's case was considered, two questions were deliberated at length: one as to Peggy's possible placement; the other as to the aims of her treatment.

The idea of placement was rejected for three main reasons. Firstly, it was felt that the support which Peggy's mother received from various sources, such as the Social Services, the Clinic Nursery, friends and relations, formed an extensive network which would hopefully prove effective in preventing Peggy's being killed. Secondly, it was difficult to envisage at that time how a placement could have been achieved at all without the cooperation of this mother, who, in spite of all her ambivalent feelings towards her child, would in all probability have fought any battle to prevent her child being taken away from her. Thirdly, a separation between the mother and her child was thought likely to prove damaging to Peggy's development. (So far as it had been possible to establish this development from observable behaviour, it was normal, even though great concern was voiced as to how long Peggy's responses would remain normal). It was felt that Peggy's attachment and ties to her mother were already established and that it would be impossible for her to accept a new mother. In short, it was too late for placement.

responseSet.title: The Importance of an External Event in the Early Treatment of a Fifteen-Year-Old Anorexic Girl: “A Sheep, Twin Lambs and a Christmas Card”
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Importance of an External Event in the Early Treatment of a Fifteen-Year-Old Anorexic Girl

“A Sheep, Twin Lambs and a Christmas Card”

Lynn Barnett

Lynn Barnett

120 Belsize Lane
London, N.W.3.

Lynn Barnett  

Background

When I first met Marilyn I was confronted by a thin, wan and rather politely frozen girl of fifteen-and-a-half. She had mousy, short straight hair and large eyes. She spoke softly and I had to change rooms in order to hear her voice above the traffic noise. Her appearance was alarming. Her heels did not meet the back of her shoes and the gap between her neck and her collar and tie was many inches. She was pale, bluish and cold. She was of average height, just above the 25th percentile, but her weight was below even the 3rd percentile for a girl of her age and height. She was referred for psychotherapy following two periods of hospitalisation, one of a week, the other of a month. The latter had been terminated by her twice running away and then refusing to go back to hospital. The treatment aim in hospital, where she had been on a special anorexic programme, had been to return her to her original weight of 7½ stone (she weighed only 5 stone 11½ lbs. when she was admitted) and to help her overcome her fear of eating. Marilyn agreed to twice weekly psychotherapy on an outpatient basis in a clinic separate from the hospital, while expressing resentment that such help would only mean getting her to eat which she said was the last thing she wanted to do. It was explained that psychotherapy would have a broader aim, which was to try and help her understand herself and her anxieties as well as what her non-eating meant for her.

Social History

From her social history it was clear that Marilyn shared all the typical features of anorexic patients as reported in the literature (Bruch (1974), Cohen (1977), Crisp (1977), Kalucy (1973), Tustin (1958)). She came from an intellectual family, both parents being teachers of a “precise science”. She was intelligent and consistently achieving 80% and 90% in all her subjects at school. Her parents married as students, having been the head girl and boy of their respective schools. Mother had never had another boyfriend. She was a very emotionally controlled woman who thought everything out carefully before talking. She kept the house spotlessly clean and the family running like clockwork in all their very many activities. She had developed a painful back condition when Marilyn was about 18 months old and had spent much time flat on her back in bed. Marilyn's father, very successful professionally, was rather passive in his domestic role. He shared with Marilyn a passion for violent exercise, e.g. squash, and unlike his wife, was very gregarious outside the home.
